question: Both C. diff risk and doxy PEP involve antibiotics. How does the guidance around antibiotic use differ between the two documents?
answer: Both C. diff risk and doxy PEP involve antibiotics, but the guidance around antibiotic use differs between the two documents. In the [FS-Cdiff-HealthcareProfessionals-508.pdf] document, the guidance focuses on C. diff infection and high-risk antibiotics for the individual patient, while in the [AntibioticSafety-Patients-P.pdf] document, the guidance includes both C. diff risk and doxy PEP as part of comprehensive sexual health approaches, emphasizing that antibiotics can cause harm and are not always the best option for treating C. diff infection.

Always assess the individual patient, use your clinical judgment, and follow your institution’s treatment guidelines and protocols when applicable. Higher-risk antibiotics that are more likely to predispose your patient to C. diff infection include: • Clindamycin • Fluoroquinolones (e.g., ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin) • Third/fourth generation cephalosporins (e.g., cefepime, ceftriaxone, cefdinir, cefixime) Prescribe the most targeted and safe antibiotic. • In patients with a history of C. diff infection, avoid the use of higher-risk antibiotics when other effective therapy is available. • If your patient reports a penicillin allergy, determine whether they are truly allergic to decrease unnecessary use of higher-risk antibiotics. Use the shortest effective antibiotic duration. FOR PATIENTS Antibiotics Can Cause Harm Antibiotics are responsible for almost 1 out of 5 emergency department visits for adverse drug events. Antibiotics are the most common cause of emergency department visits for adverse drug events in children under 18 years of age. To learn more about antibiotic prescribing and use, visit www.cdc.gov/antibiotic-use.
